analysis.one_liner: Removes the federal overtime pay exemption for truck drivers and other motor carrier employees.
analysis.headline: The bill sits in the House Education and Workforce Committee with no action since its referral on March 6, 2025, and has only 3 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law exempts most trucking employees from overtime pay rules that apply to other workers, so drivers can work long hours beyond 40 a week with no extra pay. This bill would delete that exemption from the Fair Labor Standards Act, making covered motor carrier employees eligible for time-and-a-half pay for hours past 40. It was introduced in March 2025 and referred to committee, where it has not advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Truck drivers and other motor carrier employees. Currently, federal law exempts most of these workers from overtime rules, so they can be required to work very long hours with no pay premium beyond their regular wage. Deleting the exemption would make them eligible for time-and-a-half pay after 40 hours a week, and could also give carriers a financial reason to limit extreme schedules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Truck drivers and motor carrier workers

how_it_helps.text: Deletes paragraph (1) of Section 13(b) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, which exempts 'seamen' and motor carrier employees from overtime requirements, thereby extending overtime protections to covered trucking employees [S2].
The bill is titled the 'Guaranteeing Overtime for Truckers Act' and its stated purpose is to remove the overtime wages exemption for certain employees [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Trucking companies and motor carriers, who would owe time-and-a-half wages for hours past 40 that they currently pay at straight time. Some of that cost could be passed on through shipping rates, and freight prices feed into the cost of goods generally.

drawbacks.text: Trucking firms would face higher payroll costs for hours past 40, and those costs could be passed to shippers and consumers through higher freight rates [S2].

Restructuring carrier scheduling and pay systems to comply would take time and money, and some carriers may shift more freight to non-employee arrangements such as independent contractors, who are not covered by the overtime rules this bill changes [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to drivers is direct and substantial: overtime pay for the long hours that are common in the industry, plus a payroll incentive for carriers to reduce punishing schedules that contribute to fatigue and safety risk. The main cost is higher freight operating expenses, some portion of which reaches consumers through prices. The bill's effect would depend on enforcement and on how many carriers reclassify drivers to avoid coverage, which the bill does not address.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on March 6, 2025, and no further action has been taken [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Van Drew introduced the bill on March 6, 2025, joined by Rep. Takano, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce [S1].
The full action history shows only introduction and committee referral, with no markup, no vote, and no referral to a second chamber [S4].
Three members have cosponsored the bill: two House Democrats and one House Republican [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost, because the bill has not moved; trucking companies continue operating under the existing overtime exemption.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo continues; no outcome yet

for.role: Sponsor, House Education and Workforce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee.

for.name: Rep. Mark Takano

sides.party_line_note: The bill is bipartisan in sponsorship — a Republican sponsor and a Democratic original cosponsor, with two more Democrats and one more Republican cosponsoring — and no one has opposed it on the record because no vote has occurred.

industries.note: The bill removes their exemption from federal overtime rules, so they would owe time-and-a-half pay for hours past 40 that they currently pay at straight time. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs against drivers' interest in overtime pay, though some of the cost would reach consumers through freight rates.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has had no committee action in months and only 3 cosponsors. Most bills at this stage in this committee never receive a markup or floor vote; unless the committee schedules action or cosponsorship grows substantially, the bill is likely to die at the end of this Congress.
